artworks.title: Gaea
artworks.description: A ceiling painting by the German classicist Anselm Feuerbach at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna. It presents Gaia, the primordial mother of the earth, as a serene figure enthroned in the heavens, part of the decorative program Feuerbach created for the academy in his final years.

artworks.title: Tellus in the Aion Mosaic
artworks.description: A Roman floor mosaic showing Aion, god of eternal time, standing within the ring of the zodiac, while the earth mother Tellus — the Roman counterpart of Gaia — reclines beside him with children often interpreted as the four seasons. Excavated at Sentinum in Italy, the mosaic is now in the Glyptothek in Munich.

artworks.title: Gaia on an Attic red-figure cup
artworks.description: Detail from an Attic red-figure vessel of the fifth century BC in which Gaia rises from the earth as a half-figure — the primordial mother made visible at the edge of the painted surface. Classical vase-painters rarely isolate her as a standalone portrait; here she appears as the living ground from which gods and heroes emerge.

artworks.title: Gaia Entrusts Erichthonius to Athena
artworks.description: A Roman marble relief in the Louvre (Ma 579) staging the Attic foundation myth: Gaia rises from the ground to hand the infant Erichthonius to Athena, with Hephaestus looking on. The earth mother becomes the midwife of Athens — the primordial goddess folded into the city's own origin story.

artworks.title: Victory, Janus, Chronos, and Gaea
artworks.description: A Mannerist allegory by Giulio Romano in which Gaea reclines among personifications of victory, beginnings, and time. The primordial earth is no longer a Hesiodic genealogy figure alone but a Renaissance emblem of the world's body, painted for the Mantuan court that made Romano Raphael's heir in mythological invention.

popCulture.title: Gaia hypothesis
popCulture.creator: James Lovelock
popCulture.description: Lovelock named Earth's living system Gaia — the primordial mother rewritten as a scientific metaphor for a self-regulating planet.

popCulture.title: Gaia
popCulture.description: Environmental and New Age language still calls the Earth Gaia — Hesiod's first mother as the everyday name for the living world.
